intro: A monthly headline price is not necessarily a monthly total. The amount can change with medication type, dose, membership, labs, shipping, insurance approval, or a multi-month commitment. This page compares what {{LIVE_PROVIDER_COUNT}} providers published on July 23, 2026 and marks unstated terms instead of estimating them.

HealthRX tops the evidence score with the broadest published cost record; its $99/month figure is tied to a 12-month plan, with $133/month advertised otherwise. yourEra remains the clearest low-commitment self-pay listing — separate $99 and $169 starting prices, included shipping, and a stated no-long-term-contract policy — while Trimi's $99 headline is tied to an annual plan and Gala's $179 figure is likewise described with a yearly subscription.
The comparison is commercial information only. A licensed clinician must determine medical eligibility, and compounded drugs are not FDA-approved.

pages.h1: Insurance support or self-pay GLP-1 telehealth?
intro: Insurance support and insurance coverage are different. A telehealth company can check benefits, help with paperwork, or submit a prior authorization, but the plan still controls formulary rules, approval, and out-of-pocket cost. Self-pay programs trade that uncertainty for a published cash price, often with a commitment or compounded-drug limitation.

Found is the insurance-support winner in this set because it publishes a free insurance check and carrier support. yourEra and Trimi are clearer self-pay comparators. Shed describes both insurance and cash-pay paths, but its published starting price can change with medication and dose.
None of these commercial paths establishes medical eligibility. Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, and plan coverage for a drug or indication can change.
pros: Separates navigation help from actual coverage
Shows a self-pay fallback beside insurance-support options
Keeps plan-specific and eligibility caveats visible

pages.h1: Review time is not delivery time: compare seven online GLP-1 timelines
intro: Provider pages often compress review, pharmacy processing, and delivery into one impression. The archived evidence does not. HealthRX states physician file review within 24 hours and free overnight shipping. AgelessRx states shipping within 3–5 business days. Wellorithm and Enhance.MD state delivery concepts without a delivery window. Serena Health states shipping 24–48 hours after approval and delivery within 3–5 business days.

These are snapshots, not service-level agreements. Ask what event starts each clock, which pharmacy dispenses, how tracking works, what happens after delays or missed delivery, and whether state rules alter fulfillment. A faster number does not establish medical eligibility, product availability, or better care.

pages.h1: Found vs yourEra: insurance support, self-pay terms, and cancellation compared
intro: Found and yourEra present two different ways to organize an online weight-management purchase. Found publishes an insurance-navigation path alongside self-pay memberships and says it can perform a free insurance check and work with carriers. Its offer terms then separate the membership from several possible charges: GLP-1 medication, some other medication, laboratory work, copays, coinsurance, deductibles, and services fulfilled outside the Found platform can sit outside the quoted subscription. yourEra presents a self-pay catalog instead. Its checked page advertises compounded semaglutide from $99 per month and compounded tirzepatide from $169 per month, says no insurance is required, and lists the visit, medication when prescribed, supplies, ongoing management, care messaging, and shipping as program inclusions. The comparison is therefore not simply $99 versus $99. It is an insurance-navigation membership with plan-dependent layers versus a publicly described self-pay bundle. Every figure is a July 23, 2026 first-party snapshot, not a quote, coverage promise, prescription promise, or statement that a program is appropriate for a particular person.

The cancellation record also differs. Found's offer-terms page, last updated August 13, 2025 when checked, gives plan-level billing and renewal detail. It lists a $129 monthly CORE plan; quarterly CORE billing as two $348 payments for a six-month original commitment; a $594 six-month CORE option; a $199 pay-monthly self-pay PLUS option; and, for members using insurance for medical care, a $39 monthly PLUS subscription or a $199 annual PLUS subscription. Those fees do not all buy the same thing, and the page states different renewal mechanics. It also says cancellation is available by email or through the account portal, becomes effective within 24 hours, and should occur before the current term ends to stop renewal. Its refund section supplies a narrower boundary: membership-fee refunds may apply within three days of original purchase or before the first consultation, while renewal payments are non-refundable and medications or lab kits cannot be returned or refunded once dispensed or shipped. yourEra's public page uses plainer flexibility language—no long-term contracts and pause or cancellation through the portal at any time—but does not expose the same cutoff, refund, or already-shipped-order detail. More words do not make Found cheaper, and fewer words do not make yourEra unsuitable; the disclosed terms simply support different prepayment checks.

HealthRX and AgelessRx appear only as benchmark context. HealthRX's checked page shows $133 per month on a three-month semaglutide plan and $99 per month on a 12-month plan, plus separate tirzepatide figures; it also states no insurance is required, identifies HSA/FSA eligibility, and describes physician evaluation and overnight shipping. AgelessRx's checked page lists $199 per month for compounded semaglutide plus B12, $249 per month for compounded tirzepatide plus B12, and a distinct $159-per-month yearly oral-drops offer. It says major cards and HSA/FSA cards are accepted and shipping is free. Card acceptance is not a tax-eligibility, coverage, or reimbursement decision. Neither benchmark receives ownership of this Found-versus-yourEra page. The direct decision remains insurance-navigation architecture versus a public self-pay bundle. Compare the selected cart, amount due now, plan term, medication inclusion, laboratory line, consultation charge, renewal amount, cancellation method, and refund boundary side by side. Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, and FDA says they are not reviewed before marketing for safety, effectiveness, or quality. A licensed provider retains prescribing authority. Clinic Scout compares published commercial evidence only—not outcomes, medical quality, treatment choice, or individual eligibility. Verify current enrollment and offer terms directly with the provider.

A cancellation must be submitted at least 72 hours before the next billing or shipment event to affect that cycle. Current-period charges remain due, and the cancellation generally stops future charges rather than reversing an existing one.
faq.q: How does Shed describe automatic renewal and cancellation?

faq.a: Shed's general subscription terms say charged subscription fees are non-refundable and list missed follow-ups, unused services, late cancellation, and cancellation before the minimum commitment among non-refund cases. pages.h1: Trimi vs Shed: advertised prices, included services, and subscription terms compared
intro: Trimi and Shed make different commercial promises visible. Trimi's checked homepage leads with a compact flat-price bundle: compounded semaglutide at $99 per month and compounded tirzepatide at $125 per month on annual plans, with the same price at every dose. The page says one membership covers the medication, clinician visits, ongoing check-ins, and free shipping. Shed's product page presents a broader catalog and payment-path story, including insurance or cash-pay wording, branded and compounded options, and a pricing card that lists medication, supplies, member support, and shipping. Its price display is not one clean number. The checked page shows 'Starting at $149/month +' in one section, $199 per month in a later pricing card, and site banners advertising compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide at other figures. Shed's terms add another relevant layer by identifying $199 semaglutide and $299 tirzepatide as the current standard monthly rates after the minimum term for multi-month subscriptions. This page does not select the most favorable number. It records each context and tells the reader to verify the selected product, term, and cart before payment.

The contract evidence reverses the visibility pattern. Trimi's homepage clearly labels the lowest prices as annual-plan rates but does not publish the annual billing schedule, early-cancellation process, cutoff, or general refund calculation in the checked homepage content. That makes its bundle easy to understand at the headline level and incomplete at the commitment level. Shed's terms are much more explicit. They say medication programs renew automatically every 28 days or monthly depending on the program, impose a two-full-month minimum, and require cancellation at least 72 hours before the next billing date or scheduled shipment for the request to affect that cycle. General subscription fees are described as non-refundable once charged. The multi-month section says cancellation is available after the minimum term through the portal, an email cancellation link, or support; shipped cycles are treated as used; cancellation does not automatically trigger a refund; and an eligible amount for unfulfilled cycles may be calculated after used months are repriced at the applicable month-to-month rate. The terms also describe narrower exceptions. Those rules are commercially useful because they answer what happens after checkout. They do not prove that Shed's total is lower, that every plan uses the same cadence, or that a particular refund request will be approved.

Gala GLP-1 and Wellorithm appear only as benchmark context. Gala's checked page presents compounded GLP-1/GIP at $179 per month and labels the calculation as a yearly subscription plan; it also states that compounded GLP-1 is not FDA-approved. Wellorithm's checked page presents compounded semaglutide starting at $147 and compounded tirzepatide starting at $249, says no insurance is required, and includes free-shipping language. Neither benchmark receives ownership of this page, and neither price is treated as a quote for another plan. The Trimi-versus-Shed decision is narrower: a compact annual-plan bundle versus a multi-product offer backed by more visible subscription terms. Audit that obligation on a billing calendar: mark the enrollment timestamp, installment dates, renewal anniversary, shipment cycles, dispatch notices, prepaid balance, repricing formula, cancellation cutoff, submission proof, and acknowledgment email. Save the selected SKU, cart, invoice, courier identifier, card descriptor, and plan-length disclosure together. This catches timing exposure that an amortized monthly headline hides. There is no medical winner. Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, and FDA says they are not reviewed before marketing for safety, effectiveness, or quality. FDA recommends obtaining a prescription and using a state-licensed pharmacy. A licensed provider decides whether to prescribe. Prices, pharmacies, service areas, products, and terms can change after this July 23, 2026 check. Clinic Scout compares source-supported commercial evidence only; verify current terms directly.

pages.h1: HealthRX vs AgelessRx: compare price terms, review clocks, and shipping evidence
intro: HealthRX and AgelessRx both publish self-pay pathways for compounded GLP-1 products, but their lowest visible numbers describe different purchases. HealthRX's checked page advertises compounded semaglutide from $133 per month on a three-month plan and references $99 per month on a 12-month plan. It separately presents term-qualified tirzepatide pricing. AgelessRx's checked page displays several product formats and billing periods: compounded semaglutide injection, compounded tirzepatide injection, and a compounded oral-drops option. The $159-per-month headline belongs to the yearly oral-drops offer, not every format. A responsible head-to-head therefore starts with product, route, billing period, amount due today, and total scheduled obligation—not a subtraction between two isolated headlines. Prices and offers were checked July 23, 2026 and can change.

The operational evidence also uses different clocks. HealthRX states that an independent U.S. board-certified physician reviews a file within 24 hours and, if clinically appropriate, writes a prescription. It then states free overnight shipping from a licensed 503A pharmacy. AgelessRx states licensed U.S. clinician review, ongoing messaging, state-licensed U.S. pharmacy fulfillment, and free discreet shipping within 3–5 business days. None of those phrases alone supplies a common application-to-door estimate. Review, prescription routing, pharmacy processing, carrier handoff, and delivery are distinct stages. Ask each provider which event starts its published window and what happens when a prescription changes, a shipment misses its estimate, or the destination cannot be served.

Wellorithm and Enhance.MD appear only as benchmark context. Their checked pages provide different first-month, recurring-price, service-area, laboratory, and support disclosures; those figures are not quotes for HealthRX or AgelessRx. The direct decision remains HealthRX versus AgelessRx: compare the selected product, amount due now, plan term, renewal amount, medication and supplies, clinician follow-up, shipping, cancellation path, refund terms, and state eligibility. Provider HSA/FSA language does not determine tax eligibility, reimbursement, or a plan administrator's decision. Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, and FDA does not review them for safety, effectiveness, or quality before marketing. A licensed clinician decides whether to prescribe. No program is a medical winner; verify current commercial terms directly.

pages.h1: GLP-1 shipping and clinician review: compare what each process record reveals
intro: A telehealth fulfillment path is a chain of events, not a single speed number. This four-row comparison looks for two narrow kinds of public evidence: clinician-review visibility and shipping-process visibility. HealthRX's accepted row states independent physician file review within 24 hours and free overnight shipping. AgelessRx states free discreet shipping in 3–5 business days and mentions licensed U.S. clinician review without a review duration in the accepted row. Wellorithm states free direct-to-door shipping while dispatch and delivery timing are not stated. Enhance.MD states that medication is shipped to the door and describes a 12-week cadence, but no delivery window. Those statements do not share one starting event, so they are not combined into an intake-to-door race.

Read every row as an event map. Intake may precede clinician review; a decision may precede prescription routing; pharmacy processing may precede carrier handoff; delivery follows the carrier stage. A published clock belongs only in the stage its wording supports. For AgelessRx, Wellorithm, and Enhance.MD, clinician-review timing is Not stated in the accepted rows. For Wellorithm, dispatch and delivery timing are Not stated. For Enhance.MD, the delivery window is Not stated. Missing clocks stay visible because replacing them with estimates would create a speed claim that the source record does not support. Record the stated trigger beside every duration. If the trigger is absent, mark it Not stated as well; a numerical band without a defined starting event cannot be aligned confidently with another provider's band. Keep cadence, processing, dispatch, transit, and arrival in separate columns. That structure prevents a refill interval from masquerading as delivery time and prevents a shipping phrase from becoming a claim about clinician review.

The frozen scores remain unchanged. HealthRX carries the highest accepted shipping-transparency and medical-oversight scores in this set, but that is an evidence finding, not a statement about clinical quality, medical suitability, prescription approval, guaranteed speed, safety, or outcomes. AgelessRx supplies a stated delivery band. Wellorithm makes free direct-to-door shipping visible without an elapsed window. Enhance.MD makes home shipping and a cadence visible without a carrier window. Each pattern tells a shopper which operational questions remain. Prices and program fields were checked through July 23, 2026 and can change. Verify current offers and enrollment terms directly.
